paras: The dynamiting of a Black church in Wellston, Oklahoma, took place on a Saturday night in early August 1915, when unknown persons exploded a stick of dynamite under the town's "negro church." The blast damaged the building but injured no one, and no clue to the dynamiter was found. Oklahoma papers reported it as an "echo" of the mob lynching of Ed Berry at Shawnee the day before.

According to the Wellston dispatch, a mob at Shawnee had lynched Ed Berry on the preceding Friday, a man the dispatch called "the negro ravisher" and who, it said, had made "confessions." The same report said there was "considerable race feeling" throughout the region as a result of the confessions and the lynching.

On Saturday night, unknown persons set off a stick of dynamite beneath the Black church at Wellston. The explosion "aroused the town" and damaged the building considerably, tearing off some siding and splintering a section of the floor about twelve feet square. No deaths or injuries were reported.
When the dispatch was sent on Monday, August 9, no clue to the identity of the dynamiter had been secured. No report of an arrest, investigation or later development appears in the coverage.

The Oklahoma City Times ran the Wellston dispatch on its front page on August 9 under the headline "Negro Church Is Dynamited," with a subhead calling it an "Aftermath of Lynching at Shawnee." The Daily Ardmoreite printed the same text word for word the next day on page 4, headlined "Negro Church Dynamited After Shawnee Lynching." Both versions reported the damage plainly and without comment on the bombing itself, while describing the lynched Berry as a "ravisher" and framing the attack as a by-product of regional race feeling.
No coverage of the bombing has been found in the Black press.
